subject: Science
title: The Fundamental Unit of Life
summary: This chapter builds the cell from the ground up: who discovered it, what the cell theory says, how the plasma membrane and cell wall control what moves in and out, what the nucleus and cytoplasm contain, and what each organelle does. It is the base chapter for every biology topic that follows in Classes 9 to 12.

exam_profile.weightage: Biology in Class 9 Science typically carries about 20 marks of the 80-mark theory paper, spread across the four biology chapters. This chapter is one of the most heavily tested of the four — expect at least one long-answer or case-based question built around it every year.

question_types.note: Identify an organelle from its function (suicide bags, powerhouse), name the scientist who discovered cells or proposed the cell theory, or pick the correct term for a cell process (endosmosis, exosmosis, plasmolysis).
Pairs a structural fact (e.g. plant cells have a cell wall) with the correct functional reason (rigidity, no bursting in hypotonic medium).
Define one term, or give one function of one organelle, or state one difference between two related structures.
Compare two structures (plant vs animal cell, diffusion vs osmosis, rough vs smooth ER) or explain one process in 3–4 sentences.
Draw and label a labelled diagram of a plant or animal cell, or explain osmosis with the three conditions (isotonic, hypotonic, hypertonic) and a real-life example each.
A short passage on a lab activity (raisins in water, onion peel plasmolysis, or a cell organelle malfunction) followed by 3–4 sub-questions.

hot_topics: Cell theory and who proposed each part of it
Plasma membrane — selective permeability, diffusion, osmosis, endosmosis/exosmosis, plasmolysis
Difference between plant cell and animal cell
Mitochondria as the powerhouse of the cell
Lysosomes as the suicide bags of the cell
Rough ER vs smooth ER, and Golgi apparatus function

sections.heading: 5.1 What Are Living Organisms Made Up Of?
sections.body:
Every living thing you can name — a mango tree, an earthworm, a human being — is built from the same basic unit: the cell. Robert Hooke was the first person to see and name cells. In 1665, using a self-made microscope, he examined a thin slice of cork (dead bark tissue) and saw small, empty, box-like compartments. He called them 'cells' because they reminded him of the small rooms monks lived in.

What Hooke actually saw were the cell walls of dead cork cells; the living contents had dried up long before. It took better microscopes and more careful observation, over the next two centuries, for scientists to work out that cells are not empty boxes at all — they are the living, functioning units of every organism, and every organism, from a single bacterium to a whale, is built from one cell or from many cells working together.

An organism made of a single cell (like Amoeba, Paramecium or a bacterium) is called unicellular; that one cell carries out every life function — nutrition, respiration, excretion, growth and reproduction — on its own. An organism made of many cells (like a human being or a neem tree) is multicellular; here, groups of cells specialise: some form muscle, some form nerve, some form skin, and they cooperate to keep the whole organism alive. This is why the cell is called the structural and functional unit of life — every structure of the body is built from cells, and every function of the body is carried out by cells.
sections.tip: A one-mark question often asks 'who discovered the cell' — the answer is Robert Hooke (1665), not Robert Brown (who discovered the nucleus) or Leeuwenhoek (who first saw a living cell).

sections.heading: 5.2 What is a Cell Made Up Of? How Do We See Cells?
sections.body:
Cells are too small to see with the naked eye — most cells range from about 1 micrometre to a few hundred micrometres. Some cells are visible without an instrument: the egg of a hen is a single, extremely large cell packed with stored food (yolk), and the longest cell in the human body is the nerve cell, which can be over a metre long though extremely thin. As a rule, though, cells need magnification to be studied, and the story of the cell is really the story of better microscopes.

In 1674, Antony van Leeuwenhoek, using a simple microscope he ground and polished himself, became the first person to see and describe a living cell — free-swimming organisms in pond water. Robert Brown discovered a dense spherical structure inside the cell in 1831 and named it the nucleus. Building on decades of such observations, two German scientists put forward the first two parts of the cell theory: Matthias Schleiden (1838), a botanist, stated that all plants are composed of cells, and Theodor Schwann (1839), a zoologist, extended this to animals and proposed that the cell wall is a unique feature of plant cells. Together they proposed the cell theory: all living organisms are composed of cells and the cell is the basic unit of life. In 1855, Rudolf Virchow added the crucial third part: all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula) — cells are not spontaneously created but divide to form new cells. Later, with the electron microscope, scientists discovered that the cell is bound by a membrane made of lipids and proteins, which refined the cell theory further: all organisms are composed of cells and cell products, and new cells are formed from pre-existing cells.
sections.tip: Keep the three names and their exact contribution separate — Schleiden (plants), Schwann (animals), Virchow (new cells from pre-existing cells). This is one of the most repeated one/two-mark questions in the chapter.

sections.heading: 5.3 Structural Organisation of the Cell
sections.body:
Every cell, however different it looks under a microscope, has three basic parts working together: the plasma membrane, which forms the cell's outer boundary and controls what enters and leaves; the nucleus (or, in some cells, a nucleoid region), which holds the genetic material and directs the cell's activities; and the cytoplasm, the jelly-like fluid inside the membrane in which the nucleus and all the organelles are suspended and where most of the cell's chemical reactions take place.

Not every cell has a well-formed nucleus enclosed by a membrane. On this basis, cells are divided into two kinds. In a prokaryotic cell, the genetic material (a single circular DNA molecule) lies directly in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid, with no nuclear membrane around it; prokaryotic cells are also smaller (1–10 micrometres), lack most membrane-bound organelles, and their only membrane-bound structure is the cell membrane itself — bacteria and blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) are prokaryotes. In a eukaryotic cell, the genetic material is enclosed within a well-defined nucleus by a nuclear membrane, the cell is larger (5–100 micrometres), and it contains a full set of membrane-bound organelles — mitochondria, ER, Golgi apparatus and, in plants, plastids. All organisms other than bacteria and blue-green algae — protists, fungi, plants and animals — are eukaryotes.
sections.tip: A very common short-answer question: 'Differentiate between prokaryotic and animal cells' or 'list two differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells' — always mention size, the nuclear membrane, and membrane-bound organelles.

sections.heading: 5.4 Plasma Membrane — Structure and Diffusion
sections.body:
The plasma membrane (also called the cell membrane) is the outermost boundary of the cell in an animal cell, and it lies just inside the cell wall in a plant cell. It is made of lipids and proteins, is flexible, and is porous enough to allow the automatic movement of some substances across it without the cell spending energy — this property is called selective/differential permeability: it allows some materials to pass through while blocking others.

Movement of substances across the membrane happens mainly by diffusion: molecules of a substance move on their own, from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration, until the concentration becomes uniform, without the cell using any energy. Gases move by diffusion — oxygen enters a cell by diffusion (because the cell keeps using it up, so its concentration inside always stays lower than outside) and carbon dioxide leaves a cell by diffusion for the same reason.

Osmosis is a special case of diffusion — it is the movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration (a dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (a concentrated solution), through a selectively permeable membrane, without the cell spending energy. Depending on the concentration of the solution surrounding a cell relative to the concentration inside the cell, three situations arise:

  • If the medium outside the cell has a higher water concentration than the cell (a hypotonic solution), water moves into the cell by osmosis — this is called endosmosis. A cell placed in pure water swells up.
  • If the medium outside has the same water concentration as inside (an isotonic solution), there is no net movement of water — the cell's size stays the same.
  • If the medium outside has a lower water concentration than inside (a hypertonic solution), water moves out of the cell by osmosis — this is called exosmosis. A cell placed in a concentrated salt or sugar solution shrinks.

In plant cells, exosmosis causes the cytoplasm to shrink away from the cell wall — this is called plasmolysis, and it can be reversed if the cell is placed back in water. This is exactly what is seen when raisins are placed in plain water (they swell, endosmosis) versus in a concentrated sugar or salt solution (they shrink, exosmosis), and it is why a wilted vegetable becomes firm again when kept in water.
sections.tip: Boards love a diagram-plus-explanation question: 'Explain endosmosis, exosmosis and isotonic solution with one example each.' Memorise the raisin/onion-peel example for each of the three cases — it is the standard illustration examiners expect.

sections.heading: 5.5 Cell Wall
sections.body:
The cell wall is found only in plant cells (and in fungi and bacteria), not in animal cells. It lies outside the plasma membrane and is mainly made of cellulose, a complex sugar that gives strength to plants. Besides cellulose, plant cell walls may also contain pectin and other polysaccharides.

The cell wall gives the plant cell a fixed, rigid shape and provides structural strength, which is why plants can stand upright without a skeleton. It also protects the cell from mechanical injury and from infection, and it is freely permeable, letting most substances pass through easily to reach the plasma membrane.

The cell wall is also what stops a plant cell from bursting even when a very large amount of water enters it by endosmosis in a hypotonic medium: as water enters, the cell swells, but the rigid wall resists further expansion, so the cell becomes turgid (firm) instead of bursting — this turgor pressure is what keeps leaves and stems upright and crisp. An animal cell, having no wall, would simply burst under the same condition. When a living plant cell is placed in a concentrated (hypertonic) solution, water moves out and the cytoplasm shrinks and pulls away from the cell wall — this is plasmolysis, and it demonstrates that the cell wall and the plasma membrane are separate structures.
sections.tip: A frequently asked short question: 'Why do plant cells not burst when they absorb a lot of water by osmosis, but animal cells do?' Answer with the presence/absence of a rigid cellulose cell wall, and the resulting turgor pressure.

sections.heading: 5.6 Nucleus
sections.body:
The nucleus is a large, spherical, membrane-bound organelle that is usually located in the centre of the cell. It is separated from the cytoplasm by a double-layered nuclear membrane, which has pores that allow the transfer of material between the nucleoplasm (fluid inside the nucleus) and the cytoplasm. In a non-dividing cell, the nucleus shows a dense, thread-like network called chromatin material; when the cell is about to divide, the chromatin condenses to form rod-shaped, thicker structures called chromosomes.

Chromosomes carry genetic information in the form of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) molecules. Each segment of DNA that codes for one protein, and thereby controls one particular characteristic (trait) in an organism, is called a gene. Genes are therefore the functional units of chromosomes; they control the transfer of hereditary characteristics from parents to offspring. The nucleus also contains one or more small, dense, spherical bodies called nucleoli, which are involved in ribosome formation, and it directs and controls all the cell's activities — including cell division, since it decides when and how a cell will divide to form new cells.

In prokaryotic cells there is no nuclear membrane, so the DNA-containing region is called a nucleoid rather than a nucleus. Some highly specialised cells, such as the mature red blood cells of mammals, lose their nucleus entirely once fully formed.
sections.tip: Do not confuse chromatin and chromosomes — chromatin is the loosely coiled, thread-like form seen in a non-dividing cell; chromosomes are the same material tightly coiled and thickened, visible only during cell division.

sections.heading: 5.7 Cytoplasm and Cell Organelles
sections.body:
The cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance that fills the cell between the nuclear region and the plasma membrane. It is the site of most of the cell's chemical activities, and it is where the various organelles are suspended.

The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a large network of membrane-bound tubes and sheets running through the cytoplasm, connecting the nuclear membrane to the plasma membrane. There are two kinds: rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) has ribosomes attached to its surface, which gives it a granular, rough appearance; because ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis, RER helps manufacture proteins for export from the cell. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) has no ribosomes on it; it helps synthesise fats/lipids, which, along with proteins made by RER, help build the cell membrane (a process called membrane biogenesis). In liver cells, SER also plays a role in detoxifying poisons and drugs.

The Golgi apparatus (discovered by Camillo Golgi) consists of a system of membrane-bound, fluid-filled flat sacs called cisternae, stacked parallel to one another. The material synthesised near the ER is packaged into vesicles by the Golgi apparatus, which then either stores it, modifies it further, or sends it to its target inside or outside the cell (secretion). It also forms lysosomes.

Lysosomes are small, spherical, membrane-bound sacs filled with digestive enzymes made by RER; these enzymes can break down all organic material — old, worn-out organelles, food particles and foreign invaders such as bacteria. Lysosomes act as the cell's waste-disposal system, keeping the cell clean. When a cell is damaged or dies, lysosomes may burst and their enzymes digest the cell's own components — for this reason lysosomes are nicknamed the 'suicide bags' of the cell.

Mitochondria (singular: mitochondrion) are rod-shaped or oval organelles bound by a double membrane, with the inner membrane folded into structures called cristae, which increase the surface area for chemical reactions. Mitochondria have their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins and can divide independently of the cell — a feature called autonomous organelles. Their key function is cellular respiration: they break down food (glucose) to release energy in the form of ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the energy currency of the cell — which is why mitochondria are called the 'powerhouse of the cell'.

Plastids are found only in plant cells. They are of three main kinds: chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll (and carotenoid pigments) and are essential for photosynthesis; chromoplasts contain pigments other than chlorophyll (yellow, orange or red) and give colour to flowers and fruits; and leucoplasts are colourless plastids that mainly store food such as starch, oils and protein. Like mitochondria, plastids have their own DNA and ribosomes.

Vacuoles are storage sacs for solid or liquid contents, bound by a single membrane. Animal cells have many small, temporary vacuoles. Plant cells, in contrast, have one large, permanent central vacuole that can occupy 50–90% of the cell's volume; it is filled with cell sap and maintains the turgor pressure of the cell, giving mechanical support. In Amoeba, a temporary structure called the food vacuole forms around ingested food and contains the digestive enzymes that break it down; in some fresh-water protozoans, a contractile vacuole pumps out excess water to maintain osmotic balance.
sections.tip: For a 5-mark 'match the organelle to its function' or diagram-based question, keep the nicknames sharp: mitochondria = powerhouse, lysosomes = suicide bags/scavengers, Golgi apparatus = packaging and dispatch unit, ER = transport network.

sections.heading: 5.8 Cell Division
sections.body:
New cells are formed from pre-existing cells by cell division, and this happens by two processes, depending on need. Mitosis is the type of cell division that occurs during growth and repair of tissue in the body. A single parent cell divides once to produce two daughter cells, and each daughter cell is genetically identical to the parent cell (same chromosome number). Mitosis is the basis of growth in multicellular organisms, replacement of worn-out cells, and healing of wounds.

Meiosis is the type of cell division that occurs only in reproductive organs, to produce gametes (sperm and egg cells, or pollen and ovules in plants). One parent cell divides twice in succession to produce four daughter cells, and each daughter cell has exactly half the number of chromosomes as the parent cell (this halving is why the offspring formed after fertilisation, when a sperm and egg fuse, has the normal, full chromosome number again — half from each parent).
sections.tip: A common one-mark trap: mitosis gives 2 cells with the same chromosome number, meiosis gives 4 cells with half the chromosome number. Link mitosis to 'growth and repair' and meiosis to 'formation of gametes' when asked for the significance of each.

key_terms.definition: All living organisms are composed of cells and cell products; the cell is the structural and functional unit of life; and new cells arise only from pre-existing cells, proposed jointly by Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow.
An organism made of a single cell, which alone performs all life functions, e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium, bacteria.
An organism made of many cells, with groups of cells specialised for different functions, e.g. plants and animals.
A cell with no nuclear membrane around its genetic material (a nucleoid instead of a nucleus) and generally no membrane-bound organelles, e.g. bacteria.
A cell with a well-defined, membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and ER.
The property of the plasma membrane that allows some substances to pass through while blocking others.
The movement of particles of any substance from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, without using cell energy.
The movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (concentrated solution) across a selectively permeable membrane.
The shrinking of the cytoplasm of a plant cell away from its cell wall when the cell loses water by exosmosis in a hypertonic (concentrated) medium.
Chromatin is the loose, thread-like form of DNA and protein seen in a non-dividing nucleus; it condenses into thick, rod-shaped chromosomes when the cell is about to divide.
A unit/segment of DNA on a chromosome that codes for one protein and controls one hereditary characteristic.
Double-membraned, rod-shaped organelles with folded inner membranes (cristae) that carry out cellular respiration to release energy as ATP; called the powerhouse of the cell.
Membrane-bound sacs of digestive enzymes that break down waste material and worn-out cell parts; called the suicide bags of the cell.
Plant-cell-only organelles of three types — chloroplasts (photosynthesis), chromoplasts (colour), and leucoplasts (storage) — each with their own DNA.
A stack of membrane-bound, fluid-filled sacs (cisternae) that packages, modifies and dispatches materials made near the endoplasmic reticulum.
A membrane-bound storage sac; plant cells have one large central vacuole holding cell sap and maintaining turgor pressure, animal cells have small, temporary ones.

formula_sheet.name: Cell theory (three parts)
formula_sheet.expr: All organisms are made of cells and cell products → the cell is the structural and functional unit of life → new cells arise only from pre-existing cells
formula_sheet.note: Schleiden (plants, 1838) + Schwann (animals, 1839) + Virchow (new cells from old, 1855)

formula_sheet.name: Diffusion
formula_sheet.expr: Higher concentration → Lower concentration (no energy used)
formula_sheet.note: applies to gases, e.g. O<sub>2</sub> in and CO<sub>2</sub> out of a cell

formula_sheet.name: Osmosis
formula_sheet.expr: Water moves from higher water concentration (dilute) → lower water concentration (concentrated), across a selectively permeable membrane
formula_sheet.note: a special case of diffusion, applies to water only

formula_sheet.name: Endosmosis
formula_sheet.expr: Cell in hypotonic solution → water moves IN → cell swells
formula_sheet.note: plant cell becomes turgid; animal cell may burst

formula_sheet.name: Exosmosis
formula_sheet.expr: Cell in hypertonic solution → water moves OUT → cell shrinks
formula_sheet.note: in a plant cell this shrinkage of cytoplasm from the wall is plasmolysis

formula_sheet.name: Isotonic solution
formula_sheet.expr: Water concentration outside = water concentration inside → no net movement of water

formula_sheet.name: Mitosis
formula_sheet.expr: 1 parent cell → 2 daughter cells, same chromosome number as parent
formula_sheet.note: for growth and repair of body tissue

formula_sheet.name: Meiosis
formula_sheet.expr: 1 parent cell → 4 daughter cells, half the chromosome number of parent
formula_sheet.note: occurs only in reproductive organs, to form gametes

diagrams.title: Labelled diagram of a plant cell
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a large rectangular/oval outline for the cell wall, with a thinner membrane just inside it for the plasma membrane. Draw a large central vacuole taking up most of the cell, with a thin layer of cytoplasm pushed to the edges. Place a nucleus (with nucleolus) near one side, and scatter labelled ovals for mitochondria and green plastids (chloroplasts) in the cytoplasm; add a small network of lines near the nucleus for the ER. Label all seven parts: cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, vacuole, mitochondria, chloroplast.

diagrams.title: Labelled diagram of an animal cell
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw an irregular rounded outline for the plasma membrane (no cell wall, so the edge should look less rigid than the plant cell's). Place a centrally located nucleus (with nucleolus) and fill the cytoplasm with small, scattered mitochondria, a Golgi apparatus (a stack of curved sacs near the nucleus), a network of ER lines, and a few small vacuoles. Label: plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum.

diagrams.title: Osmosis set-up: raisin/potato-cup experiment
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three beakers side by side. In the first, a raisin/plant tissue in distilled water with an arrow pointing INTO the cell, labelled 'endosmosis — cell swells (hypotonic medium)'. In the second, the same tissue in a solution of the same concentration as the cell sap, with no arrow, labelled 'isotonic — no change'. In the third, the tissue in strong salt/sugar solution with an arrow pointing OUT of the cell, labelled 'exosmosis — cell shrinks (hypertonic medium)'.

diagrams.title: Mitochondrion — internal structure
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw an oval outline with two membranes: a smooth outer membrane and a folded inner membrane. Draw 3–4 finger-like folds of the inner membrane projecting into the interior and label them 'cristae'. Label the fluid-filled space inside as 'matrix', and note beside the diagram that cristae increase the surface area for respiration.

ncert_questions.a: Robert Hooke discovered cells in 1665. He examined a thin slice of cork under a self-made microscope and observed small, honeycomb-like, empty compartments, which he named 'cells' after the small rooms (cellulae) monks lived in. What he actually saw were the dead cell walls of cork tissue.

ncert_questions.q: Why is the cell called the structural and functional unit of life?
ncert_questions.a: Every living organism is built up of cells; even the smallest structures of the body (tissues, organs) are made of cells, which gives the cell its structural role. At the same time, every activity that occurs in the body — nutrition, respiration, excretion, movement, reproduction — is actually carried out inside cells by their organelles, which gives the cell its functional role. Because the cell is both the basic building block and the basic working unit of life, it is called the structural and functional unit of life.

ncert_questions.q: How do substances like CO2 and water move in and out of the cell? Discuss.
ncert_questions.a: Small, uncharged molecules like CO<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> move across the plasma membrane by simple diffusion, from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration, without the cell using energy — CO<sub>2</sub>, produced continuously inside the cell, diffuses out where its concentration is lower, and O<sub>2</sub>, consumed continuously inside the cell, diffuses in where its concentration is lower. Water crosses the membrane by a special type of diffusion called osmosis: it moves from the side with higher water concentration (dilute solution) to the side with lower water concentration (concentrated solution), through the selectively permeable plasma membrane, again without using cell energy.

ncert_questions.q: Why is the plasma membrane called a selectively permeable membrane?
ncert_questions.a: The plasma membrane is called selectively (or differentially) permeable because it does not allow all substances to cross it equally — it permits some molecules (such as water, O<sub>2</sub>, and CO<sub>2</sub>) to pass through freely by diffusion or osmosis, while restricting or completely blocking the passage of other, usually larger or charged, substances. This selective control lets the cell take in what it needs and keep out what could harm it.

ncert_questions.q: Fill in the gaps: (a) Amoeba obtains its food through a process called ____. (b) The membrane which allows the movement of some substances through it and does not allow certain other materials to move through it is called a ____ membrane.
ncert_questions.a: (a) Amoeba obtains its food through a process called endocytosis (it engulfs food particles using temporary finger-like extensions called pseudopodia, which then form a food vacuole). (b) selectively (or differentially) permeable membrane — the plasma membrane, which allows some substances to cross while blocking others.

ncert_questions.q: Which type of cell division is required for growth and repair of body tissue?
ncert_questions.a: Mitosis is the type of cell division required for the growth and repair of body tissue. In mitosis, one parent cell divides once to give two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent and to each other, allowing the number of cells in a tissue to increase (growth) or damaged cells to be replaced (repair).

ncert_questions.q: Diffusion plays a major role in the movement of a lot of substances into and out of the cell. Explain this role with a few examples.
ncert_questions.a: Diffusion moves substances automatically from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated, without the cell spending energy, making it a simple, economical way to exchange materials with the surroundings. Examples: (i) Oxygen, continuously used up in respiration, stays at a lower concentration inside the cell than outside, so O<sub>2</sub> diffuses in. (ii) Carbon dioxide, continuously produced by respiration, is higher inside, so it diffuses out. (iii) Small food molecules and waste products also move in and out of cells down their concentration gradients.

ncert_questions.q: What would happen to the life of a cell if there was no Golgi apparatus?
ncert_questions.a: Without a Golgi apparatus, the cell would have no system to package, modify and dispatch the proteins and lipids made by the endoplasmic reticulum. Materials meant for secretion (enzymes, hormones) could not be packaged into vesicles and sent out, and materials needed inside the cell could not reach their correct destination. Lysosomes, which form from the Golgi apparatus, would also not form, so the cell would lose its main waste-disposal system. Secretion and internal transport would break down and the cell would stop functioning normally.

ncert_questions.q: Which organelle is known as the powerhouse of the cell? Why?
ncert_questions.a: The mitochondrion is known as the powerhouse of the cell. It carries out cellular respiration, breaking down food (glucose) in the presence of oxygen to release energy, which is stored in the form of ATP (adenosine triphosphate) molecules. This ATP is used by the cell to power all its other activities, so the mitochondrion supplies the cell's usable energy, just as a powerhouse supplies electricity — which is why it earns this name.

ncert_questions.q: Where do the lipids and proteins constituting the cell membrane get synthesised?
ncert_questions.a: Proteins are synthesised on the ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER). Lipids are synthesised on the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER). Both these products then move together to help in the formation (biogenesis) of the cell membrane and other cell membranes.

ncert_questions.q: How does an Amoeba obtain its food?
ncert_questions.a: Amoeba is a unicellular organism that has no fixed shape. When it comes near a food particle, it puts out temporary finger-like extensions of its cell surface called pseudopodia ('false feet'), which surround and engulf the food particle from all sides. The engulfed food, along with a little surrounding water, becomes enclosed within a food vacuole inside the cell, where digestive enzymes break it down and the digested nutrients are absorbed into the cytoplasm. This process of taking in food using pseudopodia is called phagocytosis/endocytosis.

Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration (a dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (a concentrated solution), through a selectively permeable membrane, without the expenditure of any energy by the cell. It is a special type of diffusion in which only water molecules move.

pyq.q: Who discovered the living cell for the first time?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Robert Hooke saw dead cork cells in 1665; Leeuwenhoek, in 1674, was the first to see and describe living cells (in pond water).

pyq.q: Which organelle is called the 'suicide bag' of the cell?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down waste and, when the cell is damaged, digest the cell's own components — hence 'suicide bags'.

pyq.q: The chromosome number is halved in which type of cell division?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Meiosis produces four daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number of the parent cell, and occurs only in reproductive organs.

pyq.q: A plant cell placed in a concentrated sugar solution will show:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: A concentrated (hypertonic) external solution draws water out of the cell (exosmosis), and the cytoplasm shrinks away from the rigid cell wall — plasmolysis.

pyq.q: Which part of the cell is correctly described as 'the powerhouse of the cell'?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration and release energy as ATP, the cell's usable energy currency.

pyq.q: Which of these is a prokaryotic organism?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Bacteria lack a nuclear membrane around their DNA (they have a nucleoid instead), so they are prokaryotic; Amoeba, yeast and Paramecium are all eukaryotes.

pyq.q: Rough endoplasmic reticulum appears 'rough' because it has:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Ribosomes studded on its outer surface give the rough ER its granular, rough appearance under the microscope; these ribosomes make proteins.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Plant cells do not burst even when kept in a highly hypotonic (dilute) solution for a long time. Reason (R): The rigid cellulose cell wall resists the expansion caused by water entering the cell, allowing turgor pressure to build up instead of the cell bursting.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The cell wall's rigidity is exactly why endosmosis makes plant cells turgid rather than causing them to burst, unlike animal cells which lack a wall.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Mitochondria and plastids can divide on their own, independent of the cell. Reason (R): Both these organelles possess their own DNA and ribosomes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Having their own genetic material and protein-making machinery is exactly what allows mitochondria and plastids to grow and divide independently of the cell's own division cycle.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Diffusion of oxygen occurs into the cell. Reason (R): Oxygen is continuously used up in cell respiration, so its concentration inside the cell always stays lower than outside.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Diffusion always moves a substance from higher to lower concentration; the cell's own consumption of O2 is what keeps the internal concentration low and drives inward diffusion.

pyq.q: Name the scientist who proposed that all animals are made of cells, and state the year.
pyq.answer: Theodor Schwann, a German zoologist, proposed in 1839 that all animals are made up of cells; he also noted that the cell wall is a feature unique to plant cells and not found in animal cells.

pyq.q: Give two differences between a plant cell and an animal cell.
pyq.answer: (i) A plant cell has a rigid cell wall made of cellulose outside the plasma membrane; an animal cell has no cell wall. (ii) A plant cell usually has one large, permanent central vacuole; an animal cell has small, temporary vacuoles, if any. (Additional valid points: plastids are present only in plant cells; mature plant cells rarely show centrioles, which are present in animal cells.)

pyq.q: What is plasmolysis? Give one everyday example where it is observed.
pyq.answer: Plasmolysis is the shrinking of the cytoplasm of a living plant cell away from its cell wall, caused by the loss of water through exosmosis when the cell is placed in a concentrated (hypertonic) external solution. Example: raisins or dried apricots placed in a strong sugar or salt solution do not swell, and fresh green leafy vegetables sprinkled with salt wilt and lose their crispness because water moves out of their cells.

pyq.q: Name the organelle that packages materials made by the endoplasmic reticulum, and state one function of the packaged material.
pyq.answer: The Golgi apparatus packages materials synthesised near the ER into membrane-bound vesicles. These vesicles may store the material, modify it further, or transport it to be secreted out of the cell (for example, digestive enzymes secreted by gland cells) or delivered to other parts of the cell.

pyq.q: Differentiate between diffusion and osmosis.
pyq.answer: Diffusion: movement of particles of any substance (solid, liquid or gas) from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration; does not necessarily need a membrane; can occur in any medium (air, water). Osmosis: movement of only water/solvent molecules, specifically from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to lower water concentration (concentrated solution); must occur across a selectively permeable membrane; osmosis is really a special, restricted case of diffusion that applies only to water/solvent movement through a membrane.

pyq.q: State the three parts of the cell theory and name the scientists associated with each part.
pyq.answer: (i) All plants are made up of cells — Matthias Schleiden, 1838. (ii) All animals are made up of cells, and the cell wall is unique to plant cells — Theodor Schwann, 1839. Together, Schleiden and Schwann proposed that all living organisms are composed of cells and that the cell is the basic unit of life. (iii) All cells arise from pre-existing cells (cells divide to form new cells; they are not spontaneously created) — Rudolf Virchow, 1855.

pyq.q: Explain why lysosomes are called the 'suicide bags' of the cell.
pyq.answer: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs filled with powerful digestive enzymes, made by the rough endoplasmic reticulum, that can break down almost all organic material — worn-out cell parts, ingested food, and invading microbes — and so keep the cell clean. Under normal conditions this activity is tightly controlled. But when a cell is damaged or its metabolism is disturbed, the lysosomal membrane can burst, releasing these enzymes into the cytoplasm; the enzymes then digest the cell's own organelles and structures, effectively destroying the cell. Because the same organelle that cleans up the cell can also destroy it from within, lysosomes are nicknamed the cell's suicide bags.

pyq.q: What are plastids? Name their three types and one function of each.
pyq.answer: Plastids are double-membraned organelles found only in plant cells, containing their own DNA and ribosomes. (i) Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis, making food for the plant. (ii) Chromoplasts contain pigments other than chlorophyll (yellow, orange, red) and give colour to flowers and fruits, helping attract pollinators/seed dispersers. (iii) Leucoplasts are colourless and store food reserves such as starch, oils and proteins.

pyq.q: Draw a well-labelled diagram of a typical plant cell. Explain any three ways in which it differs from an animal cell.
pyq.answer: [Diagram: a plant cell showing, from outside in, the cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm with a large central vacuole, a nucleus with nucleolus, and organelles such as mitochondria and chloroplasts, all clearly labelled — see the diagrams section for how to draw it.] Three differences from an animal cell: (i) A plant cell has a rigid cellulose cell wall outside the plasma membrane; an animal cell has no cell wall, only a plasma membrane. (ii) A plant cell typically has one large, permanent central vacuole occupying most of the cell and maintaining turgor pressure; an animal cell has small, scattered, temporary vacuoles. (iii) Plastids (chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts) are present in plant cells but absent in animal cells.

pyq.q: What is osmosis? Describe endosmosis, exosmosis and the isotonic condition, giving one example of each.
pyq.answer: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (concentrated solution), through a selectively permeable membrane, without the cell using energy. Endosmosis: cell in a hypotonic solution — water moves in, cell swells — e.g. dry raisins in plain water swell up. Exosmosis: cell in a hypertonic solution — water moves out, cell shrinks; in a plant cell the cytoplasm pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis) — e.g. a raisin in concentrated sugar/salt solution shrivels. Isotonic condition: solute concentration outside equals that inside, so there is no net water movement and cell size stays unchanged — e.g. red blood cells in normal saline neither swell nor shrink.

pyq.q: Describe the structure and functions of the mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum.
pyq.answer: Mitochondria: rod-shaped or oval organelles bound by two membranes; the inner membrane is folded inward into finger-like cristae, which increase the surface area for chemical reactions. The fluid-filled space inside is the matrix. Mitochondria carry their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make some proteins and divide on their own. Their main job is cellular respiration — breaking down food to release energy stored as ATP; this is why they are the powerhouse of the cell. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER): a network of membrane-bound tubes and sheets running from the nuclear membrane to the plasma membrane. Rough ER has surface ribosomes and makes proteins; smooth ER has none and makes lipids. Proteins from RER and lipids from SER together build new cell membranes, and in liver cells SER also helps detoxify drugs and poisons.

pyq.q:
A teacher placed three identical potato cups (hollowed-out potato pieces, like small bowls) in three beakers: Cup A in distilled water, Cup B in a concentrated salt solution, and Cup C in a solution with the same solute concentration as the potato cells' own cell sap. After two hours, the students measured the water level in each cup.
(i) In which cup would the water level rise the most, and why?
(ii) In which cup would the water level fall, and why?
(iii) In which cup would the water level stay roughly the same?
(iv) Name the process responsible for the change in Cup A.
pyq.answer: (i) Cup A (distilled water) — distilled water is hypotonic to the potato cells' cell sap, so water moves into the potato cells and further into the cup cavity by endosmosis, raising the water level most. (ii) Cup B (concentrated salt solution) — the salt solution is hypertonic to the cell sap, so water moves out of the potato cells into the surrounding solution by exosmosis, and the water level in the cup falls. (iii) Cup C — the surrounding solution is isotonic to the cell sap, so there is no net movement of water in either direction, and the water level stays roughly unchanged. (iv) Endosmosis (osmosis of water into the cells because the external medium is hypotonic).

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow: A cell biologist observes a cell under an electron microscope. It has no nuclear membrane, its genetic material lies free in the cytoplasm as a single circular strand, it is only about 2 micrometres long, and it shows no mitochondria or Golgi apparatus.
(i) Is this cell prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Give one reason from the passage.
(ii) What is the region containing the genetic material in such a cell called?
(iii) Name one organism that would show this type of cell.
(iv) Give one structural feature that IS present in this cell despite the missing organelles.
pyq.answer: (i) Prokaryotic — because it has no nuclear membrane around its genetic material (any one of: small size, no mitochondria/Golgi is also acceptable). (ii) The nucleoid. (iii) A bacterium (e.g. Escherichia coli) or a blue-green alga (cyanobacterium). (iv) The plasma membrane (cell membrane) is present, since it is the one membrane-bound structure found in all prokaryotic cells.

practice_mcq.q: Who among the following first used the term 'cell'?
practice_mcq.explanation: Robert Hooke coined the term 'cell' in 1665 after observing the box-like compartments in cork tissue.

practice_mcq.q: The part of the cell theory contributed by Rudolf Virchow states that:
options: All plants are made of cells
All animals are made of cells
New cells arise only from pre-existing cells
practice_mcq.explanation: Virchow, in 1855, added that cells divide to form new cells rather than arising spontaneously.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the plasma membrane?
practice_mcq.explanation: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not at the plasma membrane; the membrane's roles are transport-related.

practice_mcq.q: A red blood cell placed in distilled water will:
options: Swell and may burst due to endosmosis
practice_mcq.explanation: Distilled water is strongly hypotonic; water enters the cell by endosmosis, and having no cell wall, the RBC swells and may burst.

practice_mcq.q: Chromatin material condenses to form chromosomes:
options: Only when a cell is about to divide
Throughout the cell's life without change
practice_mcq.explanation: Chromatin is the loosely coiled form seen in a non-dividing cell; it condenses into visible chromosomes just before and during cell division.

practice_mcq.q: Which organelle is correctly paired with its main function?
options: Golgi apparatus — packaging and dispatch of materials
practice_mcq.explanation: The Golgi apparatus packages, modifies and dispatches materials made near the ER; photosynthesis is a chloroplast function, protein synthesis a ribosome function, respiration a mitochondrial function.

practice_mcq.q: The functional segment of a chromosome that codes for a protein and controls a trait is called:
practice_mcq.explanation: A gene is a segment of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein and thereby controls a hereditary trait.

practice_mcq.q: Rough ER differs from smooth ER mainly in that rough ER:
options: Is found only in plant cells
practice_mcq.explanation: Ribosomes studded on its surface give rough ER its name and its role in protein synthesis; smooth ER lacks ribosomes and makes lipids.

practice_mcq.q: Which of these organelles has its own DNA and can divide independently of the cell?
practice_mcq.explanation: Mitochondria (and plastids) carry their own DNA and ribosomes, allowing them to synthesise some proteins and divide on their own.

practice_mcq.q: The large, permanent, fluid-filled sac that maintains turgor pressure in a mature plant cell is the:
practice_mcq.explanation: The central vacuole, filled with cell sap, can occupy up to 90% of a plant cell's volume and keeps the cell turgid.

practice_mcq.q: In Amoeba, food is engulfed with the help of:
practice_mcq.explanation: Amoeba puts out temporary finger-like extensions of the cell surface called pseudopodia to surround and engulf food particles.

practice_mcq.q: Which pair of organelles is found only in plant cells and not in animal cells?
practice_mcq.explanation: The cell wall and plastids (chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts) are unique to plant cells; the other organelles listed are common to both plant and animal cells.

practice_mcq.q: A cell placed in an isotonic solution will:
options: Show no net change in size
practice_mcq.explanation: In an isotonic solution the water concentration inside and outside the cell is equal, so there is no net osmotic movement of water and the cell's size stays the same.

practice_mcq.q: How many daughter cells are produced at the end of meiosis, and what is their chromosome number relative to the parent?
options: Two cells, half the chromosome number
Four cells, half the chromosome number
practice_mcq.explanation: Meiosis involves two successive divisions of one parent cell, producing four daughter cells each with half the parent's chromosome number.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following best explains why plant cells rarely burst even after prolonged endosmosis?
options: The rigid cell wall resists expansion and builds turgor pressure
Osmosis does not occur in plant cells
practice_mcq.explanation: The cellulose cell wall is rigid and limits how much the cell can expand, so the cell becomes firm (turgid) instead of bursting, unlike an animal cell.

common_mistakes: Writing that Robert Hooke discovered the living cell — he only saw dead cork cells and named the compartments 'cells'; Leeuwenhoek first saw a living cell.
Mixing up which scientist contributed which part of the cell theory — Schleiden (plants), Schwann (animals), Virchow (new cells from pre-existing cells) must be kept separate.
Calling osmosis and diffusion the same thing — osmosis is specifically the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane; diffusion applies to any substance and does not need a membrane.

Confusing endosmosis with exosmosis — students often reverse which one causes swelling and which causes shrinking; always link hypotonic → endosmosis → swelling, and hypertonic → exosmosis → shrinking.
Saying an animal cell has a cell wall, or that plant cells lack a cell membrane — every cell has a plasma membrane; only plant cells (and fungi, bacteria) additionally have a cell wall.
Forgetting that mitochondria and plastids have their own DNA — this single fact explains why they can divide independently and is asked directly in assertion-reason questions.
Writing 'chromosomes' when the question describes the non-dividing nucleus (should be 'chromatin'), or vice versa.
Getting the mitosis/meiosis daughter-cell counts and chromosome numbers backwards — mitosis: 2 cells, same number; meiosis: 4 cells, half the number.
strategy:
Start with the timeline of discoveries — Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Brown, Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow — and be able to state exactly what each person contributed; this alone answers several one- and two-mark questions. Next, master the plasma membrane block: diffusion, osmosis, and the three conditions (hypotonic/endosmosis, hypertonic/exosmosis, isotonic) with one worked example for each, because this is the single most examined block in the chapter and appears as MCQ, VSA, SA, LA and case-based questions alike.

Learn the organelles as a table in your head: name → one-line structure → one-line function → nickname if any (mitochondria = powerhouse, lysosome = suicide bag). Practise drawing the plant cell and animal cell diagrams from memory, labelling at least six to seven parts correctly, since a labelled diagram is worth full marks on its own in a 5-mark question. Finish with prokaryotic vs eukaryotic and mitosis vs meiosis as quick comparison tables — these are asked almost every year in some form. Since Class 9 has no year-tagged board paper, treat every question here as 'frequently asked' rather than trying to guess a specific year.
revision_checklist: Can state the cell theory in three parts with the correct scientist for each part
Can explain why the cell is called the structural and functional unit of life
Can distinguish diffusion from osmosis in one line each
Can define and give an example of endosmosis, exosmosis and isotonic condition
Can explain plasmolysis and why plant cells don't burst on endosmosis
Can list at least three differences between plant and animal cells
Can list at least two differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
Can name the function of every major organelle: nucleus, ER (rough/smooth), Golgi apparatus, lysosome, mitochondria, plastids, vacuole
Can explain why mitochondria are called the powerhouse and lysosomes the suicide bags
Can draw a labelled plant cell and animal cell diagram from memory
Can explain chromatin vs chromosomes and define a gene
Can compare mitosis and meiosis by number of daughter cells and chromosome number
Can explain how Amoeba obtains food using pseudopodia
Has revised the raisin/potato-cup osmosis experiment and can predict water-level changes
